From #434:

I'm happy to switch back, but I want to be very sure that it doesn't affect numerical stability. Can you make sure that we don't have to increase any error bounds on any of the tests?

Unfortunately, this does significantly affect numerical stability, in particular when using an algorithm for fitting that uses (expanding) line search (such as L-BFGS). With this change many of our tests that previously passed reliably now fail.
I'm assuming the issue is due to the fact that now the individual components rather than their differences are squared: x1_norm = x1.pow(2).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True). This causes overflow issues especially when using torch.float dtype, so the resulting MVNs have nan-valued loc/covar parameters. Switching to torch.double fixes many of the instability issues, but that's of course not a good solution when running on the GPU.

For exact and variational GPs, the marginal log likelihood requires computing the log determinant of the prior covariance matrix. This isn't a super expensive operation (since we get most of the terms for free from a single call to linear_cg). However, we still have to make a few calls to torch.symeig, which can add a bit of a performance hit.
If we are simply using the MLL as a loss function to optimize hyperparameters (and not for Gibbs sampling, model selection, etc.), then we don't actually care about the logdet value (just its derivatives, which we get for free from linear_cg). Therefore, we could avoid these torch.symeig calls.
I propose a gpytorch.beta_features.skip_logdet feature flag that skips the logdet computation (but still computes the correct gradient, obviously). It will be off by default.

#376 changed priors to always operate on the actual parameters (e.g noise vs. its log or inverse softplus value). In some cases we want to sample parameters from the priors, which means that we'll have to transform the samples back to the internal parameter representation. We currently have no easy way of doing this. In particular, given a model, this requires additional knowledge of the model specifics.
'Im thinking about ways of making this easier to automate. In the most general case this is hard, because (i) if a prior is on a function of two parameters that typically won't be a bijection, and (ii) if we have multiple priors that involve the same parameter it's unclear how to enforce consistency.
Let's focus on the simple case and consider only those priors and parameters for which there is a one-to-one mapping between priors and parameters, with all mappings bijective.
One simple way would be to allow to specify an "inverse closure" when registering a prior for a single parameter. For instance, for a prior on the module's noise parameter, you could imagine something like:
.register_prior("foo_prior", foo_prior, self.noise, lambda x: self.noise = x)

which would require a @setter for the noise to be defined. This of course in turn would require that the user pass in an inv_param_transform to the module (that could be made optional by just having some dictionary mapping common transformations to their inverse, e.g. {torch.exp: torch.log, torch.nn.functional.softplus: softplus_inverse...} and error out when an unknown param_transform were supplied.
Then sampling from the prior and setting the parameter values could be done like
for name, prior, _, inv_closure in self.named_priors():
    if inv_closure is not None:
        inv_closure(prior.sample())

Thoughts on this?
cc @bletham
nodes.title: Inverse parameter transforms and association with priors

tl;dr: We need to better handle the precomputed cache for train-train covariance
Say you fit a GP in standard (non-batch) mode (n x p input).

if you evaluate it in standard mode (m x p input), you're fine
if you evaluate in batch mode (b x m x p input) without having previously evaluated in standard mode, you're fine
if you first evaluate in standard mode, then in batch mode (or vice versa), an error is raised because of incompatible sizes of the train_train cache.

This is a bug, going back between the different modes should be possible.
Further, the following should be supported:

fitting a GP in batch mode (b x n x p input) and then evaluating in "standard" mode (b x m x p input)
fitting a GP in batch mode (b x n x p input)  and evaluating in batch-batch mode (b' x b x n x p input)

The only thing that should not be supported is evaluating a GP fitted in batch mode (b x n x p input) on an incompatible size (b' x n x p input, where b' != b)

Training a GP model in the very recent beta version takes significantly more time than that in the older alpha version. I tested this on a simple 1D regression task (taken from notebook) and found that the average training time in beta version is 2.32 seconds compared to 1.21 seconds in alpha version for the exact same scipt (pasted below) except the random_variables replaced by distributions. The script is run on an Intel I7 CPU @2.7 GHz (no cuda). Is this expected behavior ?
import math 
import time
import torch
import numpy as np
import gpytorch 

from gpytorch.likelihoods import GaussianLikelihood
from gpytorch.means import ZeroMean
from gpytorch.kernels import RBFKernel
# import ipdb


class GPModel(gpytorch.models.ExactGP):
	def __init__(self, train_x, train_y, likelihood, version='alpha'):
		super(GPModel, self).__init__(train_x, train_y, likelihood)
		self.mean_module = ZeroMean()
		self.covar_module = RBFKernel()
		self.version = version

	def forward(self, x):
		mean = self.mean_module(x)
		covar = self.covar_module(x)
		if self.version == 'beta':
			return gpytorch.distributions.MultivariateNormal(mean, covar)
		else:
			return gpytorch.random_variables.GaussianRandomVariable(mean, covar)

class GP(object):
	def __init__(self, train_x, train_y, version):
		self.likelihood = GaussianLikelihood()
		self.model = GPModel(train_x, train_y, self.likelihood, version)
		self.optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([{'params': self.model.parameters()}], lr=.1)
		self.mll = gpytorch.mlls.ExactMarginalLogLikelihood(self.likelihood, self.model)
		self.train_x = train_x
		self.train_y = train_y

	def fit(self, max_iterations):
		for i in range(max_iterations):
			self.optimizer.zero_grad()
			output = self.model(self.train_x)
			loss = -self.mll(output, self.train_y)
			loss.backward()
			self.optimizer.step()


if __name__ == '__main__':
	train_x = torch.linspace(0, 1, 100)
	train_y = torch.sin(train_x * (2*math.pi)) + torch.randn(train_x.size())*.2

	num_sims = 5
	all_times = []
	for _ in range(num_sims):
		start = time.time()
		gp = GP(train_x, train_y, 'beta')
		gp.fit(max_iterations=200)
		end = time.time()
		all_times.append(end - start)

Currently, model fitting requires writing a custom loop to take gradient steps. All the tutorials perform that for a fixed number of steps without any kind of smartness about how the loss / the parameter values evolve during the course of the optimization.
To make this easier for the non-expert (and to avoid writing tons of boilerplate code), I suggest we provide an (optional) wrapper for the model fitting loop that uses some reasonable convergence criteria to stop the optimization.
Given a specified model, likelihood, mll_class, train_x and train_y, calling this could be as simple as:
from gpytorch import fit_model
fit_model(model, likelihood, train_x, train_y, mll_class)

Implementation wise this would be something like the following:
def fit_model(model, likelihood, train_x, train_y, mll_class, optimizer=None, options=None, verbose=True):
    options = options or {}
    model.train()
    likelihood.train()
    mll = mll_class(likelihood, model)
    optimizer = optimizer or torch.optim.Adam(
        [{"params": model.parameters()}],
        lr=options.get("lr", 0.1), # be smarter about this
    )
    param_trajectory = {
        name: [] for name, param in model.named_parameters()
    }
    loss_trajectory = []
    converged = False
    while not converged:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(train_x)
        loss = -mll(output, train_y)
        losses.append(loss.data.clone())
        loss.backward()
        if verbose:
            print("Iter {} - MLL: {:.3f}".format(i + 1, -loss.item()))
        optimizer.step()
        for name, param in model.named_parameters():
            param_trajectory[name].append(param.data.clone())
        converged = check_convergence(loss_trajectory, param_trajectory)
    model.eval()
    likelihood.eval()

Of course we'd need to think a little harder about what check_convergence should be for the stochastic optimization algorithms used here.

nodes.bodyText:
Proposal: kernels are not responsible for lengthscales. We can introduce a separate scaling module that divides the data by lengthscales before feeding the data into the kernel
Reasoning: we do some batch-dimension hacking to get fast kernel diagonals, as well as fast batch kernels. For kernel diags - we transform the n x d data into n x 1 x d data, which then only computes kernel diagonals. For additive/multiplicative kernels, we transform the n x d data into d x n x 1 data.
There is a problem when we are using an ARD option for kernels, or when we have separate lengthscales for the different batches. If this lengthscale scaling happens before the data enters the kernel, this problem is mitigated.
In general - this would introduce a convention that kernels should not define their own parameters (which is already the case with output scales).
Rolling in the change: if we're all on board with this, we will deprecate kernel lengthscales. We will encourage users to use the lengthscale module and initialize kernels with lengthscale=False. When we're ready for a major release (and remove lengthscales completely from kernels), then the lengthscale=False kwarg won't be necessary any more.
